title: An Elephant for Charlemagne
text:
Around 797 Charlemagne, king of the Franks, sent an embassy to Harun al-Rashid, the Abbasid caliph in Baghdad, ruler of the richest empire of the age. The mission included two Frankish nobles and a Jewish merchant named Isaac, probably chosen for his languages and knowledge of the routes. The journey took years. Both noblemen died along the way.

According to the Royal Frankish Annals, Isaac returned in 801 with gifts from the caliph, among them an elephant named Abul-Abbas. Getting it to Europe was a feat: he brought it across North Africa, over the sea to Italy, and in the spring of 802 over the Alps. It arrived at Charlemagne's court in Aachen in July 802, the first elephant seen in northern Europe in centuries, and lived there until 810.

The exchanges continued. In 807 Harun's envoys brought more gifts, including a splendid tent and a brass water clock that marked the hours by dropping little balls onto a bell, with mechanical horsemen that appeared at each hour. Charlemagne's court had never seen such a device. Einhard, Charlemagne's biographer, says Harun valued Charlemagne's friendship above that of all other kings.
lesson: Goodwill between distant parties is often built with patient gestures and thoughtful gifts. Respect shown across great differences can open relations that force never could.
people: Harun al-Rashid, Charlemagne, Isaac the Jew
source: Royal Frankish Annals, years 801, 802 and 807; Einhard, Life of Charlemagne 16
caveat: Einhard's claims about the warmth of Harun's friendship are not confirmed by Arabic sources, which do not mention the embassies.
